cards.title: Four words for sadness, and what English misses
cards.body: Chereen Shurafa's claim is that Arabic's several distinct words for sadness let speakers articulate emotional states that collapse into one word elsewhere — and that clinical diagnostic categories are cruder still than ordinary language. The philosophical question underneath: is a feeling you have no word for quite the same feeling? What would you name, if you could?

cards.title: Great books are caves, not billboards
cards.body: The idea is thickness: some works unfurl in response to your attention, giving back more the longer you stay. The catch is that rewarding the careful reader usually means repelling the casual one, which is why the classics can look like a hoax from outside. He was handed the books but never told the treasure was stashed inside. Which one are you still standing outside of?

cards.title: A 5-second query, fixed by one SQLite command
cards.body: Full-text search over a 4,000-row table was taking five seconds, which is absurd for a table that small. The fix wasn't an index or a rewrite — it was running ANALYZE, which generates the statistics the query planner leans on. The query dropped to roughly 0.05 seconds. Reach for it first when a tiny table is inexplicably slow: the planner may just be guessing.

cards.title: Hormuz mines, missiles, and $91 crude
cards.body: The US struck two rocket launchers it said were about to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz; Iran answered with missiles fired at Jordan — the first exchange in over a month. Brent rose 3% to $91. Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume full-scale bombing since June's truce but hasn't, with munitions badly depleted; new sanctions on countries dealing with Iran are expected instead.

cards.title: Music Box (album)
cards.body: Music Box is the third studio album by American singer-songwriter Mariah Carey. It was released on August 31, 1993, by Columbia Records. In an attempt to appeal to a wider audience, Carey sought a radio-friendly approach for Music Box.

cards.title: Most advice fails in one of three ways
cards.body: The claim: advice is usually obvious ("don't sweat the small stuff" — if I thought it was small, I wouldn't be sweating it), true for some people and backwards for others ("be more aggressive"), or simply wrong ("live every day as if it were your last"). That leaves a narrow band that is actually good. What's the last advice that changed what you did?

cards.title: Attention doesn't just see the world — it makes it
cards.body: McGilchrist's The Matter With Things argues that the brain mechanisms which simplify the world enough for us to control it also work against truly understanding it. Attention is never pure: its aperture is narrowed by conditioning and by evolutionary necessities we've long outgrown. The whole, he insists, is never the sum of its parts. What does your attention quietly destroy while it's busy creating?

cards.title: The thumbs-up button is a bad translator
cards.body: Bailey's joke proposal for richer Netflix feedback icons — "my cat walked over the keyboard," "I am making bad choices and hatewatching this" — lands because everyone has had the thought. Nielsen's point is that we know the button is a reductive expression that'll be misread, and we press it anyway. What has every recommendation engine quietly concluded about you from that?

cards.title: Brussels revives the encryption backdoor push
cards.body: The European Commission is pushing again for encryption backdoors, this time under its ProtectEU strategy. It's the same standoff as every prior round: lawful-access demands on one side, and on the other the awkward fact that a weakness built for one government works for anyone who finds it. Worth tracking if you ship software into Europe.

cards.title: 2019 — on this day
cards.body: A sightseeing helicopter crashed in the mountains of Skoddevarre in Alta, Norway, killing all six people on board.

cards.title: MDMA's mystical states may not be the point
cards.body: With psilocybin and LSD, the deeper the mystical experience, the better the outcome tends to be. One new study of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD points elsewhere: patients do sometimes have full mystical states, but those don't appear to drive the symptom relief — the ordinary positive emotional states do. Different drug, different mechanism, and a caution against one grand theory of psychedelic therapy.

cards.title: There is no perception free of memory
cards.body: Writing in 1896, Bergson argued we never perceive the present cleanly: a thousand details from past experience mingle with the senses, and memories often supplant what's actually in front of us. Speed and convenience are what we buy with that trade; illusion is what we pay for it. If perception is mostly recall, how much of today did you actually see?

cards.title: Building websites like it's 2010, on purpose
cards.body: Evans wanted a site with many different pages and didn't like the frontend-heavy options, so she went backward: SQL database, HTML rendered on the backend, as little JS as possible. Django made that feel achievable where Go's standard library and Flask hadn't. Reach for it when the project is a lot of small pages rather than one rich app.

cards.title: Nigeria's worst violence in three decades
cards.body: Hundreds were abducted from mosques in northern Nigeria this month, and the three months through June were the country's most violent in at least thirty years. President Tinubu ordered a rescue operation for the 600 taken in Niger state, having just left for a three-week European vacation mid-campaign. His team's three-year scorecard led with economic results and stayed quiet on security.

cards.title: Launch of the Roman Space Telescope
cards.body: A new telescope has been launched into space to study the universe. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (RST) has the same size main mirror as the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) but sees 100 times more sky during each snapshot.  This is possible because when compared to HST, RST's main mirror is more curved, its secondary mirror is closer, and its main camera is larger.

cards.title: The help that keeps a child's anxiety alive
cards.body: Family accommodation is when relatives rearrange their own behavior to spare an anxious child distress: answering the same worried question for the tenth time, or quietly dropping the feared birthday party. One new study suggests the children least able to regulate their emotions pull the most accommodation from their families. Comfort given in the moment can quietly confirm the fear was right.

cards.title: Kant: kindness you feel isn't morality
cards.body: For Kant, the basis of morality is reason, not happiness. What you owe another person comes from their rational agency and inherent dignity, not from whether you happen to feel something for them. So helping the colleague who grates on you counts exactly as much as helping the friend you love. A demanding standard, and a strangely reliable one.

cards.title: The AI that didn't wait to be asked
cards.body: Agency, the initiative to act without waiting for instructions, is becoming the thing that decides how AI goes for us, and it is no longer only ours. The piece builds its case on the Hugging Face Incident from July, whose fuller details surfaced this week via METR/Redwood and OpenAI. AI used to sit in a chat window until you gave it work. What happens when it stops waiting?

cards.title: AI adoption tripled. Employment barely moved.
cards.body: Census asked hundreds of thousands of firms how AI had changed their headcount. Two years apart, the answer barely budged: 94.6% reported no change in early 2024, 95.7% in the latest supplement, even as measured AI use roughly tripled. Among firms using it, 44% say it supplemented work employees already do; 10% say it took over a task.

cards.title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the God Dionysos
cards.body: This coin depicts the god Dionysos crowned with ivy leaves on the front and holding grapes on its back. Dionysos is believed to have come from Thrace, where this coin was minted, though several Thrace cities claimed to be his birthplace. One was Maroneia, on the coast of Thrace, which was said to be named after Dionysos’s son Maron. Dionysos was the city’s protective deity and appeared on its coinage.

cards.title: A radio station as an argument for human taste
cards.body: William Goldsmith spent years building Radio Paradise, an internet station where the question of what comes next is answered by a person. Greg Easley reads it as a living argument for taste and trust — that choosing well is an art, not a problem waiting to be optimized away. What do you lose when nothing you hear was chosen for you?

cards.title: Beauvoir's test for a good relationship
cards.body: Beauvoir rejected love as two people committing forever to pre-given roles. Her better version is a mutual project: each partner backing the other's growth and change, including the changes that aren't convenient. The test stops being "do we fit?" and becomes "does this leave us both freer?"

cards.title: Where AI actually sped science up
cards.body: A METR analysis checked three fields for real acceleration. Cyber shows a lot: vulnerability reports jumped sharply in 2026 versus 2025 across cURL, OpenSSL, Firefox, Microsoft and aggregate databases. Math shows a little, with arXiv submissions doubling in some areas inside a year, though the value of that volume is hard to quantify. AI research itself is too tangled to call.

cards.title: The cognitive bill for a restricted appetite
cards.body: Sarah Berg argues that women are trained from childhood to restrict their appetite, and that the cost isn't only physical — there's a huge, hidden cognitive price attached. The essay puts hunger in the frame usually reserved for other kinds of mental load. What does thinking cost when the body is running short?

cards.title: Touch as a doorway into physics
cards.body: An Aeon video treats touch — the most ordinary of the senses — as an entry point to the deepest questions in physics and philosophy, built as a blend of words and images rather than an argument. What does it actually mean for two things to touch?
